clue.text: Classic example of feral cat running wild

indicators.note: something running wild is out of control, so the letters of the two words beside it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A stray cat dashing about untamed is offered as a textbook case of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running wild' rearranges FERAL CAT. The Classics are the five great English horse races (the Derby, the Oaks and so on), each run on the flat without jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Each English Classic, such as the Derby, is a race run without fences, so it is one instance of the type.

clue.text: In between being sentimental and pretty

indicators.note: In says the letters wanted sit inside the very next word of the clue

explanation.surface: Something is caught halfway between mawkish and attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' points inside the word 'between', where the four letters sit together; 'being' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee is the British word for something too sweet, quaint or prettified, cloyingly sentimental.

clue.text: Break into a politician's address

parts.note: read as burglary of an MP's house, but really meaning to interrupt a speech with shouted jeers

explanation.surface: Someone burgles the home of an MP.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Address' is a home in the surface but a speech in the real reading, and 'break into' means interrupt rather than burgle.
explanation.definitionFit: To barrack a speaker by shouting interruptions during a speech is exactly what this verb describes.

clue.text: Put off and fed up, having made a mistake

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word fed is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: to err is to make a mistake, so having made one is erred

explanation.surface: Someone is sick of things after slipping up and postpones them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed up' looks like the idiom for exasperated, but in this down clue 'up' is a reversal signal acting on 'fed' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To defer something is to postpone or delay it, so put off is a straight synonym.

clue.text: They hold two feet of copper hose

parts.note: a bobby is British slang for a policeman, also called a copper
hose is an old word for stockings or socks

explanation.surface: A policeman's legwear is described as holding both his feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' is police slang, not the metal: a bobby is a British police officer. Bobby socks are ankle socks worn by teenage girls in the 1940s and 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: These are a type of short sock, and a pair of socks covers the wearer's two feet.

clue.text: Firm, after rising cuts, goes to the wall

indicators.note: after places the firm's letters following the turned word
in a down clue rising means the word cuts is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A company facing spending cuts goes bust, as businesses do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes to the wall' is the idiom for going bankrupt, which suits the surface, but here it means something applied to a wall: 'rising' turns CUTS into STUC.
explanation.definitionFit: Stucco is a plaster finish spread over walls, so it is literally something that goes onto a wall.

clue.text: Noisy and unruly — otherwise perfect?

parts.note: F stands for forte, the musical direction meaning loud
lawless means disorderly and uncontrolled, unruly

explanation.surface: Something loud and wild might, in other respects, be faultless.
explanation.walkthrough: F is the musical mark forte, meaning loud. 'otherwise' links the two halves: noisy and unruly, but read another way, perfect.
explanation.definitionFit: Something perfect has no flaws at all, which is what this adjective literally says.

clue.text: Neighbourly get-together

definitions.meaning: friendly and companionable towards others, as an adjective
a party or informal gathering, as a noun

explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an adjective for sociable friendliness and a noun for a gathering such as a club party.

clue.text: Torpedo carriers ordered to base

indicators.note: ordered means put into order, so the letters of to base are rearranged

explanation.surface: Ships armed with torpedoes are commanded back to port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ordered' rearranges TO BASE. 'Ordered to base' reads as a naval command, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: German motor torpedo boats of the Second World War were known to the Allies by this name.

clue.text: Number not in style, a real eyesore

indicators.note: not in says a letter is to be removed from inside the word style

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, a number

explanation.surface: An unfashionable figure is something ugly to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not in' takes L, the Roman numeral 50, out of STYLE. The definition is a pun: a sore on the eyelid is literally an eye-sore.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling on the eyelid, so it is literally a sore on the eye.

clue.text: Fouled player retaliated

definitions.meaning: a footballer brought down by a kick from behind has been kicked in the back
struck back or responded in kind

explanation.definitionFit: To kick back is to strike back in retaliation, and a fouled footballer may have been kicked in the back.

clue.text: Vessel for a service in church

indicators.note: in puts the article and the service inside the letters for the church

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
the RAF, the Royal Air Force, is one of the armed services

explanation.surface: A container is used for a religious service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'service' looks like a church service, but it is the RAF, one of the armed forces; CE is the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A carafe is a glass bottle or jug for serving wine or water, a kind of vessel.

clue.text: Express split into clearly distinct parts

definitions.meaning: to put into words, voice clearly
jointed or divided into separate segments, as a lorry or a skeleton is

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb the word means to voice; as an adjective it describes something jointed into separate sections, like an articulated lorry.

clue.text: A foundation garment is retired on showing wear

parts.note: a bra is a woman's supporting undergarment, a foundation garment

indicators.note: retired means withdrawn or turned back, so the word is is reversed

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A worn-out old bra is finally retired, looking frayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns IS into SI; 'showing' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrasion is the gradual wearing away of a surface by friction, so it names wear.

clue.text: Turned and left

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means both soured, of food, and departed; it can also mean exploded, as a bomb does.

clue.text: Society match?

parts.note: read as a high-society marriage, but really a game played for its own sake rather than for points, such as a society might arrange

explanation.surface: A marriage between two people from high society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'match' suggests a wedding pairing, but means a game; a society's game against another club, with nothing at stake, is a non-competitive one. The Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) adds a second pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A match played with no league points at stake is called by this word, which also means amiable and sociable.

clue.text: Train wedging old coin between the points

indicators.note: wedging says one piece is driven in as a wedge between others
between places the coin inside the two compass points

parts.note: E and E are compass points, east twice
a ducat is an old gold coin of several European countries

explanation.surface: A railway train runs with an old coin stuck in the rail points.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like the railway, as do 'points', but it is a verb meaning teach, and the points are compass bearings, E for east twice.
explanation.definitionFit: To train someone is to teach or instruct them, the verb's ordinary meaning.

clue.text: Kind of shirt with frills: very tasteful

parts.note: T, as in T-shirt, names a kind of shirt
ruffles are gathered frills of fabric

explanation.surface: A frilled shirt is admired as being in the best of taste.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tasteful' suggests stylish dress, but means full of flavour: truffles, the fungus or the chocolate, are rich delicacies.
explanation.definitionFit: Truffles, the prized fungi or rich chocolates, are delicacies full of flavour, so the definition plays on taste.

clue.text: Organisation for the better

definitions.meaning: a gambler, someone who bets, uses a scheme to beat the bookmaker

explanation.definitionFit: The word means an orderly arrangement, and also a punter's scheme for winning bets.

clue.text: Expedition to the French metropolis goes round river

parts.note: a la is French for to the

indicators.note: goes round says the city's letters surround the river's

parts.note: a metropolis is a large city

explanation.surface: A French trip to a big city goes around a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expedition' looks like a journey, but here means speed or promptness, its older sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Expedition in its older sense means promptness or speed, which matches eager briskness.

clue.text: Have an inferior berth, but keep quiet

definitions.meaning: to sleep in a bed placed low down, the bottom bunk
to stay hidden and out of sight

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally means to recline near the floor, and idiomatically means to hide away and avoid notice.

clue.text: Row results from wearing an underwired bra

definitions.text: results from wearing an underwired bra
definitions.meaning: a wired bra lifts the bosom, pushing the chest up

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang for a quarrel, and read literally describes a bosom raised up.

clue.text: Bribe goes to the French in blunder

parts.note: a bung is British slang for a bribe
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A bribe paid to the French ends in a fiasco.
explanation.walkthrough: BUNG is British slang for a bribe or backhander; 'goes to' joins the pieces and 'in' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To bungle is to botch or mess up, the same as blundering; both work as nouns too.

clue.text: Point to one duke or another

parts.note: W is west, a compass point
Duke Ellington was the American jazz bandleader

explanation.surface: Someone singles out one nobleman or a different one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duke' is the jazzman Duke Ellington; add W (a compass point) to him and you get another duke, the Duke of Wellington, victor of Waterloo.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke of Wellington is a second, different duke from the jazz musician named in the wordplay.

clue.text: Steal a free ride

definitions.meaning: a ride given in someone's car without charge

explanation.definitionFit: The word means to shoplift and, in British use, a free trip in someone else's car.

clue.text: Feline connections reported

indicators.note: reported means said aloud, so the word is a sound-alike

parts.note: links are connections between things

explanation.surface: Ties to a cat family are passed on as news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' means the word for connections, LINKS, is said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: The lynx is a wild cat with tufted ears, so it is a feline.

clue.text: Accommodation move for those approaching fifty

indicators.note: move says the letters are shifted about into a new arrangement

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: People nearing fifty are advised to change where they live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'approaching fifty' reads as middle age, but just sets L (the Roman numeral 50) beside THOSE; 'move' then rearranges the six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A hostel is cheap shared lodging, a kind of accommodation, often for young travellers.

clue.text: Stay well away from work

parts.note: read as avoiding the office altogether, but really meaning to remain absent while healthy by feigning illness

explanation.surface: Advice to keep your distance from the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'well' looks like an intensifier for 'away', but means healthy: someone who is well yet stays off work is shirking.
explanation.definitionFit: To feign sickness to avoid duty is to skive while actually fit, which is what the clue describes.
